scopeReview: SPS-7.A.1–3: technologies/resources, uneven industrial diffusion, food/population/labor/class changes and demand for raw materials/markets as a contributor to imperial expansion.
varietyReview: Four assessed original stimuli: coal/canal schematic, fixed-workforce productivity, sector count/share shifts and a simplified imperial input/output network. Additional applications distinguish steam options, organization, class evidence and resource determinism.
repetitionReview: Different evidence demands and varied keys; avoids inventing historical city data, a universal start date, instantaneous water-power replacement or colonialism originating only with industry. Every option explained; difficulty uncalibrated.
referenceNote: Official scope and primary museum/archive history checked. Questions, accounts and schematics original; no historical source figure/question copied, no new student resource and no independent human-review claim.

questions.correctOption: Coal and transport access could support power and input movement, alongside capital, labor and technology.
questions.independentReview: Original hypothetical coal/canal/mill geometry checked; no invented historical city. Mechanism plausible, not a deterministic causal estimate or claim steam immediately displaced all water power.

questions.correctOption: Output per worker rises from 10 to 30 units, while the worker count remains 100.
questions.independentReview: Independently divided1000/100 and3000/100. Same product/time/total hours stated, no cross-product quantity comparison or assumption of equal distribution.

questions.correctOption: Its share falls from 80% to 40%, but its count remains 800 because total employment doubles.
questions.independentReview: Allshares80+10+10=100 and40+40+20=100. Independently calculated agriculture800/800, factory100/800, others100/400. No inference that all workers moved from farming.

questions.correctOption: Seeking raw-material supplies and markets for manufactured goods.
questions.independentReview: Historical sequence checked: industrial demand contributed to later imperial expansion, not origin of all colonialism. Fictional R/F/M nodes avoid fabricated country statistics or a claim trade alone proves domination.

questions.correctOption: Early mechanized industrialization developed in Britain and subsequently spread unevenly through connected regions.
questions.independentReview: Primary Science Museum chronology checked; no exact contested starting year or claim of universal linear superiority.

questions.correctOption: It could provide mechanical power away from suitable water-power sites, although fuel, water supply and transport still mattered.
questions.independentReview: Verified separate-condenser context without copying patent wording or claiming a water-free steam process. No instantaneous displacement of water mills.

questions.correctOption: They could support larger nonfarm populations and alter rural labor demand, alongside other demographic and economic changes.
questions.independentReview: Retains SPS-7.A.2 food/population/labor linkage without asserting mechanization alone accounts for all migration or immediate universal welfare gains.

questions.correctOption: Factories concentrate machinery and coordinated labor at a production site, often reorganizing work and control.
questions.independentReview: General historical comparison, not a claim every factory shares identical labor organization or that household industry was purely subsistence.

questions.correctOption: Changing occupational, ownership, wage and housing patterns across social groups over time.
questions.independentReview: Class change not equated with a universal improvement or with one occupational count. No actual person classified.

questions.correctOption: They connected resource areas, production centers and markets, reducing some movement constraints.
questions.independentReview: Diffusion tied to networks and uneven accessibility, not technological determinism or the claim railways originated all regional industry.

questions.correctOption: Natural resources interact with technology, investment, labor, markets and institutions rather than determining industrialization by themselves.
questions.independentReview: No ranking of inherent cultural ability or single-cause explanation. Original contrast addresses the limits of resource determinism.
